description: Lists every file open in ByteRipper: its id (pass it as `document` to the other tools — never show it to the person), `label` (what to call it to the person: the file's name, told apart from another of the same name), `link` for a file on disk (the label as a Markdown link that brings it forward in ByteRipper — write it where you name the file), name, path, size, whether it has unsaved edits, and where it is — pane A or B of a tab, or a part opened over its parent file ("part", with the parent's id, the bytes of the parent it came from, and `decoded` — what the part's bytes are to those: `LZMA`, `XOR 77`, `Read-only`…, absent for a plain copy — and `keeps_offsets`, whether byte n of the part is byte n of the source). A part is read, searched and analysed by every tool as a file of its own, from address 0, in its decoded form, and its tool panel is its own. The document the reader is in comes first and is marked `focused`. Ids last as long as the file stays open.
name: documents
title: Open documents

description: What the person at ByteRipper is looking at and pointing to: the document they are in, the caret, the selection (null when there is only a caret), and the bytes on screen. Call it when they say "this", "here" or "what I selected". In a comparison of two files it also names the other one, which scrolls with this one.
name: focus
title: Where the reader is

description: Reads bytes of an open document as it is now, unsaved edits included. `format`: "hex" (default) gives rows of 16 bytes with their address and text, as the dump shows them; "ascii" a string with "." for bytes that are not printable; "utf16le" the bytes decoded as UTF-16LE text; "u8", "u16", "u32", "u64" a list of unsigned integers in hex, little-endian unless `endian` is "big". At most 4096 bytes; a range running past the end of the file is cut there and says so.

document.description: The document's id from `documents`. Default: the focused one.

endian.description: For u16, u32 and u64. Default "little".

length.description: How many bytes. Default 256, at most 4096.

name: read
title: Read bytes

description: Shows a place in a document to the person: brings its tab forward, scrolls the dump to it and moves the caret there — selecting `length` bytes when `select` is true, which is the default when a length is given. It is a step of the navigation history, so the person's Back returns to where they were. Use it to point at what you are talking about.

document.description: The document's id from `documents`. Default: the focused one.

length.description: How many bytes the place is. Default 0: just the caret.

select.description: Select the bytes. Default: true when `length` is given.

name: reveal
title: Show bytes to the reader

description: Puts an annotation on a place in a file: a short `title` (what the bytes are), an optional `note` (why they matter, or what you found there), and the place — a `document` or a file `path`, with `offset` and `length`, or a UEFI `node` — whole, or with `offset` and `length` counted from the node's first byte: a `find_bytes` match with `node` is `node` and `node_offset`. It is listed in the Annotations window and drawn over the bytes — a dashed outline, the note when the person rests the pointer on them — whenever the file is on screen, now or after it is opened later; it is kept when the file closes. Use it both to show what bytes are while you explain them and to leave a result for the person to check — with `survey`, one on each file that matches. Whenever it is about bytes you have already annotated — a pointer and its target, a size and the stretch it names, a checksum and what it covers — annotate the other end first and pass its id in `related_to`: the person sees the relation and cannot otherwise. `reveal: true` also brings the place on screen, opening the file in a tab if it is not. In a part — a fragment panel — it goes to the file the part came out of, at the same bytes where the part keeps the file's addresses, otherwise at the bytes the part was decoded from; `from_part` says where it was in the part. A place in bytes that are not the file's own — what a compressed section decompresses to, a LENV block decoded, given as a node there or as a part of them — is kept there: the annotation answers `decoded` (the section or block, the range in its bytes, the `codecs`), the person's double-click opens those bytes in a fragment panel at the place, and the card shows the codecs as badges, so the title need not name them. A place in a module's code — a `function`, or an instruction `address`, in a Code panel given as `document` or in a module's image `node` of a dump with a stored analysis — is a code annotation: the person's double-click opens the module's Code panel at that function or instruction, the panel shows the note beside it, and the answer has `code`. Annotations go with `remove_annotations` or when the person clears them.

address.description: Or an instruction's Ghidra address in that code — the place is the instruction.

document.description: The document it is in. Default: the focused one.

function.description: A function of a module's code, by name or Ghidra entry address: annotate it in the Code panel `document`, or in the module at image `node` of the dump `document`.

node.description: Or the UEFI node it is about, e.g. "0.2.5" — inside a compressed section too.

note.description: A sentence or two: why they matter, or what was found. At most 600 characters.

offset.description: The first byte: in the document, or with `node` from the node's first byte.

path.description: Or the file it is in, by path, open or not.

related_to.description: Ids of annotations this one is about, e.g. ["a1"] for the target of a pointer. Give it whenever there is such an annotation.

reveal.description: Also bring the place on screen. Default false.

title.description: A few words: what the bytes are. At most 80 characters.

name: annotate
title: Annotate a place

description: The annotations made so far, oldest first — on every file, or on a `document` or a file `path`: id, the file's `path` (and its `document` id while it is open), `range` and/or `node`, `decoded` for a place in decompressed or decoded bytes, `title`, `note`, `related_to`, and `author: "person"` for one the person made by hand. Pages: `limit` is a ceiling — a page also stops before the answer passes the size bound and then says `truncated: "size"`; pass `next` back as `after` until it is null. A page asked for after the list changed is refused.

after.description: The `next` of the page before, to go on from where it stopped.

document.description: Only the annotations on this document's file.

limit.description: The most items one page holds — a ceiling: a page stops sooner when the answer would pass the size bound, and says so with `truncated: "size"`. Default 50, at most 200.

path.description: Only the annotations on this file.

name: annotations
title: List annotations

description: Removes annotations: the ones named in `ids`, or every one on a `document` or a file `path`, or — with `all` — every one. Relations to a removed annotation go with it.

document.description: Remove every annotation on this document's file.

path.description: Remove every annotation on this file.

name: remove_annotations
title: Remove annotations

description: Opens a file by path without putting it on screen, read-only, and returns its document id — for the tools that take `document` (`read`, `uefi_tree`, `uefi_find`…), but not for the ones that show things (`reveal`, `annotate`, panels); `show` puts it on screen. A file already open in a tab answers with that tab's id. The last eight are kept parsed; older ones are closed and opened again when asked for. A file changed on disk is read again and keeps its id.

path.description: An absolute path, or one starting with ~/.

name: open_dump
title: Open a dump in the background

description: Closes a document `open_dump` opened. Files open in a tab are the person's and are not closed.

document.description: The background document's id.

name: close_dump
title: Close a background dump

description: Opens a background document in a new tab — or brings forward the tab that already has the file — and shows `offset` there, selecting `length` bytes when given. Returns the on-screen document's id, which replaces the background one. Never opens into a pane that holds a file. A tab is a change of context: to look inside a node or a stretch of a dump that is already on screen, use `open_part`, which opens a panel in the same window instead.

document.description: The document's id.

length.description: How many bytes to select. Default 0.

offset.description: Where to show. Default: the start.

name: show
title: Put a dump on screen

description: Runs one tool that takes `document` (`uefi_find`, `uefi_node`, `uefi_at`, `read`…) on every file in `folder` (or in `paths`), opening each in the background, and returns the answers grouped by the value at `group_by` — a dotted path into the tool's answer, e.g. "total", "matches.0.start", "values.0", "chain.-1.name" (a negative index counts from the end). Each group: the value, how many files gave it, and up to ten of the files; the largest groups first. A file is named by its path from `root` — the `folder`, or the folder all the `paths` share — so files of one name in different subfolders are told apart, and `root` joined to the name is the path to open. Files a tool refused are listed under `failed`. Takes a while on many large images; reports progress. At most 200 files. Pages: `limit` is the most groups on one page, a ceiling — a page also stops before the answer passes the size bound and then says `truncated: "size"`; pass `next` back as `after`, with the same other arguments, until it is null. The next page is answered from the same run, not a new one. A group whose value is too large alone gives it as the start of its JSON text, marked `truncated: "item"`.

after.description: The `next` of the page before, to go on from where it stopped.

folder.description: A folder of dumps: files ending in .bin, .rom, .fd, .cap, .dump, .img, .scap.

group_by.description: Where in the answer the value to group by is. Default: the whole answer.

limit.description: The most items one page holds — a ceiling: a page stops sooner when the answer would pass the size bound, and says so with `truncated: "size"`. Default 20, at most 100.

paths.description: Files to survey, instead of a folder.

recursive.description: Look in subfolders too. Default false.

tool.description: The tool to run on each file.

name: survey
title: Ask one question of many dumps

description: The runs of bytes where `document` and `against` differ, in address order — compared at the same absolute offsets, unsaved edits included, as the window's A/B comparison compares. Never aligned: data that moved shows as one long run, not as a move. Runs closer than `merge_gap` matching bytes are one run; each has `start`, `end` (half-open), `length` and `differing_bytes`, which is less than `length` where matching bytes were merged in. `totals` count the whole range, whatever the page. Only bytes both files hold are compared: when the sizes differ, `tail` says where the longer file's extra bytes are, and they are not counted. With `structure` "auto" each run says `where` it is in `document`: the top-level area (region, volume, ME partition) and the deepest node that covers the run whole — a run across a boundary is placed at the node holding both sides, never split. Ids are those `uefi_node` and `me_tree` take; `where` is empty when nothing covers it. `summary: true` answers the areas instead, those with no differences too. Pages: `limit` is a ceiling — a page also stops before the answer passes the size bound, and then says `truncated: "size"`; pass `next` back as `after` until it is null. A page asked for after either document changed is refused. Reads only; nothing on screen moves.

after.description: The `next` of the page before, to go on from where it stopped.

against.description: The id of the document to compare it with, from `documents` or `open_dump`.

document.description: The first document's id from `documents`. Default: the focused one.

end.description: The first byte after the range. Default: the end of the shorter file.

limit.description: The most items one page holds — a ceiling: a page stops sooner when the answer would pass the size bound, and says so with `truncated: "size"`. Default 100, at most 1000.

merge_gap.description: At most this many matching bytes between two runs make them one. Default 16; 0 merges nothing.

offset.description: Where the compared range starts, the same in both. Default 0x0.

structure.description: Place each run in the firmware's structure, or not. Default auto.

summary.description: Answer the areas of the image with their differences instead of the runs. Default false.

name: diff
title: Byte differences

description: Shows `document` and `against` to the person as a pair — A and B side by side, their differences coloured — in the window's own comparison. A pair already on screen is brought forward; a document alone in its tab gets the other beside it; otherwise the two open in a new tab, leaving the person's tabs as they are. Answers the ids of A and B as they are on screen (a background document gets a new one). Then `reveal_diff` walks the differences. A part (`open_part`), or anything never saved, has no file to open beside another: the two open as copies of their bytes in a new tab, and the answer says `copies` — an edit there reaches neither the documents nor a parent.

against.description: The document to show beside it, as B.

document.description: The document to show as A. Default: the focused one.

name: compare
title: Show two documents side by side

description: Moves both panes of a pair `compare` showed to the next or previous difference — the step the window's own difference arrows take, with the person's grouping of nearby differences — from `from`, or from the caret. A step of the navigation history, so the person's Back returns. Answers the difference, or `found: false` at the end. `document` is either side of the pair.

document.description: A or B of the pair. Default: the focused one.

from.description: Where to look from. Default: the caret.

name: reveal_diff
title: Show the next difference

description: Every place a text or a byte pattern occurs, in one of two scopes. Without `node`: the document's bytes as they are stored, with unsaved edits — the find bar's own search — in address order, `offset`/`end` limiting the range. With `node` (an id from `uefi_tree`, `uefi_find` or `uefi_at`, or "root" for the whole image): what the UEFI tree holds at and under that node — every container opened, every compressed section searched in what it decompresses to (nested ones too), a BIOS Guard update in its assembled region, a Lenovo LENV block stored XOR-encoded decoded — and only so: a compressed stream or an encoded block as stored is not searched, nor is an ME region. Opening everything takes a few seconds on a large image the first time; the same search of unchanged bytes again — a next page — is answered from the last one. A text the file holds only compressed is found this way and not the other. `text` is looked for as ASCII, as UTF-16LE, or both (`encoding`, default both), any case with `ignore_case`; `hex` is bytes, with `??` for a byte that may be anything ("24 ?? 4D 49"). Each match: the `encoding` that matched; without `node`, `start`, `end` (half-open file addresses) and `where` it is, as `diff` places a run; with `node`, in tree order, the `node` that holds it whole (as `uefi_tree` gives it) with `node_offset`, from its first byte (its part "all"), and `body_offset`, from its body's, when the match lies in the body (its part "body", what `uefi_node_data` and `pattern_part` read by default), its `volume` and `volume_offset`, and `start`/`end` in the file — or, inside a compressed section, `in_compressed: true`, the `section` (open it with `open_part` part "decompressed") and `buffer_start`/`buffer_end` in what it decompresses to, which `uefi_node_data` reads — and `decoded` ("XOR 77") in a LENV block decoded. With `context`, a `preview` of the bytes around it — none, and `redacted: true`, in an area the flash map names MSDM, Password or Key. `total` counts every match; with `node`, `unread` lists the compressed sections that would not decompress. Matches do not overlap unless `overlapping`: "AA" in "AAAA" is two, or three with it. Pages: `limit` is a ceiling — a page also stops before the answer passes the size bound and says `truncated: "size"`; pass `next` back as `after` until it is null. `show` "compact" answers each match as where it is and no more — `node` by its id with `node_offset` and `body_offset`, or `start` — and "count" answers `total` alone. `pattern_node`, `pattern_range` and `pattern_part` take the pattern from a node's bytes instead of `text` or `hex`, the place it came from among the matches; `any` marks bytes of it that may be anything, such as an operand that holds an address. With `survey`, which dumps of a folder hold a string.

after.description: The `next` of the page before, to go on from where it stopped.

any.description: Bytes of that pattern that match anything, each "offset+length" from the pattern's start: ["0x10+4"].

context.description: Bytes before and after each match to show in `preview`. Default 0, at most 64.

document.description: The document's id from `documents`. Default: the focused one.

end.description: The first byte after the searched range. Default: the end. Not with `node`.

hex.description: Bytes to find, as hex pairs; `??` for any byte: "24 ?? 4D 49".

ignore_case.description: Letters in either case — ASCII letters of `text`. Default false.

limit.description: The most items one page holds — a ceiling: a page stops sooner when the answer would pass the size bound, and says so with `truncated: "size"`. Default 100, at most 1000.

node.description: Search what the UEFI tree holds at and under this node, decompressed and decoded; "root" for the whole image.

offset.description: Where the search of the document starts. Default 0x0. Not with `node`.

overlapping.description: Count matches that overlap one another. Default false.

pattern_node.description: Take the pattern from this node's bytes instead of `text` or `hex`.

pattern_part.description: Which bytes of `pattern_node`. Default "body". `pattern_range` counts from this part's start: a match's `body_offset` goes with "body", its `node_offset` with "all".

pattern_range.description: The stretch of the part to take, "offset+length": "0x100+0x200". Required with `pattern_node`; at most 1 MiB.

show.description: What to answer: "full" rows; "compact" rows, only where each match is; "count", `total` alone. Default "full".

text.description: A text to find. Give `text` or `hex`.

name: find_bytes
title: Find bytes or text

description: Opens a stretch of a document as a part of its own, in a fragment panel over its parent's tab — as Open Zone and the UEFI Structure panel's Open do — and answers its new `document` id. This is the way to open a node, compressed or not, or any stretch you want to read or edit: it keeps the person in the window they are in, with the parent showing behind the panel. A new tab is for switching to another context or for comparing two parts; `compare` opens one. The part's addresses start at 0, so two blocks at different addresses of two dumps compare with `diff` and `compare`; every tool that takes `document` works on it. Give `offset` and `length`, or `node` (with `part`) for a UEFI node: "all" (the default) or "body" for its bytes — a node inside a compressed section opens as what it decompressed to — "decompressed" for what a compressed section decompresses to, "decoded" for a Lenovo LENV block (or one of its entries) decoded, its XOR encoding removed. The part stays linked: edits to it stay in it until the person puts them back with Update in Parent, which for a decompressed node compresses them again. The answer says which `part` opened, and a LENV block opened without "decoded" comes with a `hint`. Asking again for a part that is already open raises its panel and answers `reused: true` with its `document` — not a second copy. `tool_panel` names the tool panel the part shows, null when none: `open_panel` with the part's `document` opens one on it. From then on the UEFI tools name the same node in the parent and the part (`counterpart`, `decoded_in`), and a call that names the parent while the focus is on the part answers with a `focus_note`. The new part takes the focus, so a call that leaves out `document` now goes to the part, and a node id belongs to the document it was listed on, the parent: give `document` (the `parent` of the answer) when you go on with that node. A part has its own tree, with its own ids: the parent's 0.3.4.1.2.5 is 0.0.5 in the decoded block. The parent must be on screen (`show` puts a background dump there). Closes with `close_dump` or by the person.

document.description: The parent's id from `documents`. Default: the focused one.

length.description: How many bytes the part is.

name.description: What the part is called. Default: the parent's name and what it is.

node.description: Instead of `offset` and `length`: a UEFI node's id.

offset.description: Where the part starts in the parent.

part.description: With `node`: the whole node, its body, what a compressed section decompresses to, or a LENV block decoded. Default "all".

name: open_part
title: Open a part

description: Every place in a firmware image that refers to an address or a GUID, in the file and inside its compressed sections, grouped by the FFS file each is in — so "which modules use this region" is one call. `guid` is written as usual and searched in its EFI byte order. `address` is a file address (or, with `relative_to` "region", an offset in the BIOS region) and is searched in the forms `forms` names: `bus` — where the BIOS region is mapped below 4 GiB, the region's end at 0x100000000, as 32 and 64 bits; `file` — the file address; `region` — the offset in the BIOS region; each little-endian, 32 bits. Address hits are chance as often as not in code: each says the `form` it matched, and none is hidden, but a shorter form is not listed apart where it only matched inside a longer one. `scope`: "all" (default), "raw" (the file as stored) or "compressed" (what the sections decompress to). Per file: `file` (its id), `name`, `guid`, `type`, `in_compressed`, and `hits` — `form`, `section` and `section_offset` in it, `file_start` where the hit has a file address. A hit in no FFS file is listed by the deepest `node` holding it. `total` counts the hits, `files` the groups. Pages: `limit` is a ceiling on files — a page also stops before the answer passes the size bound and says `truncated: "size"`; pass `next` back as `after`. With `survey`, which dumps of a folder refer to a GUID.

after.description: The `next` of the page before, to go on from where it stopped.

document.description: The document's id from `documents`. Default: the focused one.

forms.description: Which forms of `address` to search: "bus", "file", "region". Default all three.

limit.description: The most items one page holds — a ceiling: a page stops sooner when the answer would pass the size bound, and says so with `truncated: "size"`. Default 50, at most 200.

relative_to.description: What `address` counts from: the file (default) or the BIOS region.

name: refs
title: Find references to an address or a GUID

description: Read a module's stored code analysis. The module is the Code panel or tab given as `document`; or a PE32/TE image `node` of a dump (`code_modules` lists the ones with an analysis), its bytes hashed to find the analysis; or a `module` SHA-256, read from the store alone. No panel needs to be open. `what` picks the list (default "functions"): "functions"; one function's "instructions" (paged: `limit`, then `next` as `after`, until it is null) or decompiled "c"; a function's callers and callees ("references"); the instructions that "uses" an address — who calls a function, jumps to a label, or reads a global or a string; "strings"; "symbols", the named data — GUIDs, service tables, interfaces; or "post_codes", the values written to port 0x80 (what a POST card shows), each at the call that supplies it, with the functions it passes through (`via`) — `search` narrows by value — and, last, the writes whose value or port the code does not say (`unresolved`). A function's `name_source` says where its name came from: DEFAULT is Ghidra's FUN_ placeholder, ANALYSIS a name the UEFI pass read from the module (`name_reason` says from what), IMPORTED the image's own. `review_level` is how far the review has got — full, partial, decompiled, library or no_body; null in an analysis made before it was recorded — and `review_gaps` what keeps it from full: name, plate, comments, params, locals, c (a body that did not decompile), as the last publish recorded them, so a write shows in them only at the next publish; `text: "registry"` on a row or a C says it reads as its registry entry (`text_unavailable` when its entry could not be read), and `publisher_addresses` lists names there that still carry the address of the module the entry came from; `full` is a mechanical bar on those fields, not a judgement of the function: it does not look at a comment on data, at a placeholder on a register or `HASH` (that is `temporaries`), or at whether a type is right; `temporaries` the placeholder names its C still prints (uVar1, in_ECX), reported only: not a gap, and a library function can hold them, so a clean row does not mean the locals are named; a library function's `library_kind` whose library it is — edk2, amd (AGESA) or intel (FSP/RC) — and `library_entry`, the library registry entry it was matched with: `id`, `version`, and `state` — entry (the function is it), edited (changed on it since), differs (its review keeps `differences`) or conflict (its review was made on version `base`, not the current one). The answer to `what: "functions"` also carries `library`: the module's tagged library functions by kind (`edk2`, `amd`, `intel`), how many carry a registry entry (`with_entry`) and in which `state`, how many entries hold this module's current version (`installed`), how many still print a placeholder name (`with_temporaries`, reported only), and `below_bar` — the tagged functions short of the bar, counted by the gap each keeps (name, plate, comments, params, locals, return, c) — with `too_short`, bodies Function ID cannot hash, known only while the module's owner runs. `live` says whether an owner has this module's program open — the `ghidra_*` tools read that program, `code_query` reads the stored analysis — and, while it does, `unpublished_writes` whether the program holds writes the store has not got: publish to bring them across. Addresses come twice: `entry`/`address` is Ghidra's virtual address, `offset` the same byte's offset in the module, the number the hex view shows (none when read by `module` alone). To show the person a function, `open_code`; to leave a note on it, `annotate` with `function`. These are stored observations, not a live disassembly; the C is Ghidra's reading of the instructions, not the source.

after.description: The `next` of the page before; a list too long for one answer says one.

document.description: A Code panel or tab, or the dump the module is in. Default: the focused one.

function.description: A function name or Ghidra entry address, for "instructions", "c" and "references".

level.description: With `what: "functions"`: only functions at this review level.

limit.description: The most items one page holds — a ceiling: a page stops sooner when the answer would pass the size bound, and says so with `truncated: "size"`. Default 200, at most 500.

module.description: Or the module by its bytes' SHA-256, read from the store without a dump.

node.description: The module's PE32/TE image node in the dump, e.g. "0.6.4.0.0.205.2" — from `code_modules`.

recipe.description: With `module`: which analysis, when there are several. Default: the newest.

search.description: A word to narrow functions, strings or symbols by; with `what: "c"` and no `function`, text to find in every function's stored C, any case, as written.

name: code_query
title: Read a module's code analysis

description: The PE32/TE modules of a dump that have a stored code analysis: their image `node`, name, the analyses (`recipes`, newest first) and how many functions the newest found. The modules are found by their bytes — the same module in another dump has the same analysis — including those inside compressed sections, which are opened for it: seconds on a large image the first time. Read one with `code_query`, show it with `open_code`.

document.description: The dump. Default: the focused one.

name: code_modules
title: List a dump's analyzed modules

description: The shared registry of library functions: one entry per function body (its Function ID hashes), holding the review of an EDK2, AGESA (`amd`) or Intel FSP/RC (`intel`) library routine as one module published it, for every module whose function has the same body. Without `id`: the entries — `id`, `name`, `kind`, `version`, where the current version came from (`source`: module, address, revision) and how many bodies it covers (`variants`, which is not how many modules hold it) — narrowed by `search` (a part of the name) and `kind`, sorted by name. `show` lists instead `taken_out`, the bodies given back to their modules and why, or `sources`, the citations by body, narrowed the same way. Every list is paged by `limit` and `after`, and every answer says `total`, `taken_out_total` and `sources_total`. With `id`: that entry, or a taken-out one, its `review` (signature, parameters and locals by storage, plate, step comments by offset from the entry) and its `history` of versions, each with the module that published it and, for a version taken over another module's, the reason. A recorded function comes with its C but without `instructions`, `c_spans` and `c_fields`; `function_parts` says how large each is, and `part` reads one, paged. `review.body.size`, in hex at the head of the `id`, is Function ID's count of code units, not bytes: in practice the instructions without the calls. A name on a decompiler temporary (`HASH:`, `unique:` storage) stays the module's and does not reach `review.locals`. A publish offers the registry every function tagged `library.<kind>` whose review meets the bar of a finished function.

A panel of the same module already open is raised rather than opened twice. Answers the panel's `document` id, which `code_query` reads.

name: ghidra_modules

description: Opens a module for a review in Ghidra and answers its owner's `hello`: program, functions, unpublished changes. Give the PE32/TE image `node` of a dump (`uefi_find` with `name: "PE32 image"` or `"TE image"` lists them) and its `document`: its bytes go to Ghidra, whose project is made the first time — seconds for a PEIM, a minute for a large DXE driver. A module seen before opens by `module`, the SHA-256 the answer gives. Ghidra is the analysis server's when Settings ▸ Code Analysis names one, and this Mac's own otherwise. Then read, rename, type and comment with the other `ghidra_` tools and `ghidra_publish`: every ByteRipper reading shows the result. A review aims at C that reads like source — enums for constants, structures for pointer walks, comments a source would have; the MCP instructions spell the rules out.

name: ghidra_open

description: Where every module's last published analysis names a type, whole identifiers only, by its name and its tag together: `modules`, each with `module`, `name`, `revision` and `uses` — `functions` (`entry`, `name`, `in_signature`, `line_count` and the first `lines` of C, comments included), `data` typed with it or whose comment names it, the module's other `types` that name it, and `holds_the_type`. For correcting a name across the modules, before or after `ghidra_type` withdraws it. It reads the store: a module with no project here is found, and writes not yet published are not seen. `functions` counts them all; `limit` bounds how many are listed, and `truncated` says some were left out. Slow on a large store: it reads every module.

name: ghidra_type_uses
title: Find where the modules name a type

description: The module's functions as Ghidra holds them now: entry, name, name_source, size, signature, `tags`, and for a function the export writes at the library review level `library` — `edk2_name` or `tag` — and `library_kind` — edk2, amd or intel; none for a bare `library` tag. `name_contains` and `name_source` (a Ghidra source such as USER_DEFINED) narrow the list, `address_from`/`address_to` narrow it by entry. `filter: "unfinished"` keeps what a review has not passed — a parameter or a local Ghidra still names itself, or one still typed `undefined`, or no plate comment — each with `leftovers`, and `summary` says how many of how many; that filter decompiles every function, so it is slow on a large module. `leftovers.fragments` counts the register and `unique:` pieces the decompiler splits off while a review types a function — its own artefacts, which do not make a function unfinished, though a name like `uVar1` among them still prints in the C — and `fragment_names` names them; `filter: "fragments"` lists every function that has them. Paged by `offset` and `limit`; `next` says where the next page starts. `library_entry` is the function's mark and whether it is still the entry (`state`: entry, edited). While the registry reads through, a row at its entry has the entry's name and signature and `text: "registry"`, or `text_unavailable` saying why not; `leftovers`, and so `filter: "unfinished"`, stay the project's, and can list a function that reads as its entry.

address_to.description: Only functions whose entry is at or before this address.

name: ghidra_functions
title: List a module's functions

description: The spans of executable memory between neighbouring function bodies that hold anything but padding — the code the analysis never made a function of, because it cuts a function where a reference points and a body registered in a table, or reached by nothing at all, has none. Each gap says `start`, `end`, `size` and `first_bytes` (16); whether its first byte is already an `instruction` or `defined_data`; the `references` into it from outside — `all`, `data`, `code` — with up to eight `reference_targets` and, when something points in with data, `body_at`; whether a body `preceded_by_body` runs into it; and a `verdict`: `data` — what refers in reads a datum that already has its type; `body` — a data reference lands in the gap outside any datum, so something registered it (a callback, a table slot) and `ghidra_function_create` at that target makes it a function, whatever its first bytes look like; `tail` — nothing refers to it and the body before it runs into it, so it is that body's tail and belongs with it, not a function of its own; `unclaimed` — nothing refers to it and no body runs into it; `referenced` — code refers into it, which a function ought to have taken. `count` is how many gaps the module has; paged by `offset` and `limit`.

limit.description: The most items one page holds — a ceiling: a page stops sooner when the answer would pass the size bound, and says so with `truncated: "size"`. Default 200, at most 1000.

module.description: The module: the SHA-256 of its bytes, as `ghidra_modules` lists it.

name: ghidra_gaps
title: List the gaps between function bodies

description: One function as Ghidra holds it now: its signature, its `tags` and — for a function the export writes at the library review level — `library`, why: `edk2_name` for a name on the EDK2 list, `tag` for a review's library tag — and `library_kind`, whose: edk2, amd or intel; its parameters and locals with their `storage` and `first_use` (what `ghidra_rename_variable` names a local by), its plate comment, its `comments` — every comment in the body with its `address`, `kind` (plate, pre, eol, post, repeatable) and `text`, to check against a re-read of the C — what is left to name or type — a name Ghidra made up, or an `undefined` type — (`leftovers`, whose `fragments` are the decompiler's register pieces rather than missing names), and its decompiled C — fresh after every write, ahead of what the app shows until a publish. While the registry reads through, a function at its entry answers the entry's name, signature, plate, comments and C with `text: "registry"`, as the store reads it, and `publisher_addresses` lists any name that still carries the address of the module the entry came from; `parameters` and `locals` stay the project's. Any write in it makes it `edited` (`library_entry.state`): it then answers as Ghidra holds it. A publish that changes its review makes that the entry's next version, for every module that holds it, from any holder; one that does not — a name on a temporary, a label, an equate alone — leaves the entry as it is, the function reads as the entry again, and `project_names` lists a temporary's name the C does not print. `text_unavailable` says why a marked function has no `text`: the entry could not be read, or this store has no reading of the function. `summary: true` leaves the C and the equates out, for walking a module without its text. A function the decompiler refuses answers `decompile_error` and `suspects`: the parameters, locals and referenced data whose applied type is a pointer to something that is not a structure — where `PTRSUB off of non structured pointer type` comes from — so the offending symbol is named rather than bisected for.

explain.description: When the C does not come out, bisect the data the body references: each datum is let go in turn inside a transaction that is rolled back, and the ones after which the C decompiles are named under `explained`. Nothing is kept; a rollback that did not take says so and stops.

module.description: The module: the SHA-256 of its bytes, as `ghidra_modules` lists it.

summary.description: Leave out the decompiled C and the equates: signature, parameters, locals, plate, leftovers.

name: ghidra_function

description: The instructions of the function at `address`, with their bytes, references and the names of their constants (`equates`). At an instruction no function holds, as `ghidra_gaps` lists them, the code from there to the next function, and `gap` in place of `entry`. At bytes nothing has decoded, a reading of them as code with the program left as it was, `undecoded: true`, 64 rows unless `limit` says otherwise, and `stopped_by` for what ended it: not a claim that they are code. A large function comes in pages: `limit` instructions from `from`; `next` is the address to pass as `from` for the rest.

from.description: The first instruction of the page. Default: the function's first.

limit.description: The most instructions in the page. Default: all.

name: ghidra_disassembly

An empty list means no calls.

description: The type `name` three ways: as the module's program holds it (`program`), as the shared review archive holds it now (`shared`, what another review published), and as the EDK2 archive holds it (`edk2`); each is null where that place has no such type. Each has its C, `size`, and for a structure or union every field's `offset`, `size`, `name`, `type` and `comment`, with `packing` and `packing_value`. `same` says whether the program's and the shared one agree. A name and its tag find each other — `NAME` finds `_NAME` and the other way round; `resolved` gives the name that answered. `found` says whether any of the three has the type, and `near` lists close names when none does. Read the types `ghidra_publish` reports in `type_conflicts` with it, and bring yours in line with `ghidra_type`.

name: ghidra_type_definition

description: The types the program holds — what a review defined and what the module used — with `kind` (struct, union, enum, typedef, function, pointer, array), `size` and `source` (the program, or the archive the type came from). `contains` narrows by name, `kind` by what a type is — one kind, or several separated by commas — `source` by origin, and `builtin` adds Ghidra's own types, left out by default. `sources` lists every origin the program's types hold — the reviews' archive included — so `source` is named rather than guessed. Paged by `offset` and `limit`; `total` is how many match. With `contains`, `in_archives` lists what the review archive and EDK2 hold under that name and the program does not yet: it needs no definition, and is taken in when first used.

description: Names the function at `address`. Any address inside a function names that function, and the answer says which it matched (`matched: "entry"` or `"containing"`); an address that carries a label is refused — a label is named with `ghidra_label`, which is not this call. A name Ghidra would make unique (`Foo_1`) is refused: choose another. `reason` says why, as the app shows it.

address.description: The function's entry address, or any address inside it.

module.description: The module: the SHA-256 of its bytes, as `ghidra_modules` lists it.

name: ghidra_rename
title: Name a function

description: Names the label at `address` — a jump target the C prints as `LAB_<address>`, which is a step of the flow: an error exit, a loop's head, the place a structure starts being read. `ghidra_rename` names functions only: given an address inside one it renames the function, so a label needs this call. A function's entry, and an address no instruction starts at, are refused. An empty `name` deletes the label there.

module.description: The module: the SHA-256 of its bytes, as `ghidra_modules` lists it.

reason.description: Why this name, in a few words.

name: ghidra_label
title: Name a branch label

description: Makes a function at `address`: code only a table points at — a slot of a services table, a member of a PPI or a protocol — which no call names, so Ghidra left it outside any function and `ghidra_rename` finds nothing there. Disassembles it first if needed. With `name`, names it as `ghidra_rename` would. A function already there is answered as it is. An address inside another function's body is refused, naming that function: a function made there splits the body it belongs to. Undo a split with `ghidra_function_delete` or `ghidra_function_merge` first.

module.description: The module: the SHA-256 of its bytes, as `ghidra_modules` lists it.

reason.description: Why this name, in a few words.

name: ghidra_function_create
title: Make a function where Ghidra made none

description: Removes the function at `address` — its entry or any address inside it. The bytes stay disassembled; what the function said about them is gone, and the next publish drops it from the analysis. This is how a split is undone: `ghidra_function_create` refuses to make a function inside another function's body, and a body the analysis split on a conditional jump is removed here and the right one made again.

address.description: The function's entry, or any address inside it.

module.description: The module: the SHA-256 of its bytes, as `ghidra_modules` lists it.

name: ghidra_function_delete
title: Remove a function

description: Removes the local variables of the function at `address` — the decompiler's and the review's, or with `names` only those — and decompiles it again, answering what was cleared (`locals`: each one's name, storage, first use and type, to give back what matters with `ghidra_rename_variable`) and whether the C now decompiles (`decompiles`), with the error when it does not. The candidate for a function the decompiler refuses, such as two symbols assigned to one variable, where names it kept stand in the way: name the two its error names before clearing everything. It is not a guarantee, and what is cleared goes: read the function again and name what matters. While the C still fails, the answer names `suspects` — the parameters, locals and referenced data typed as a pointer to something that is not a structure, which is where such a failure comes from.

address.description: The function's entry address, or any address inside it.

module.description: The module: the SHA-256 of its bytes, as `ghidra_modules` lists it.

names.description: Only these locals. Default: every one.

name: ghidra_function_locals_reset
title: Let a function's locals go

description: Gives the body of `from` to `into` and removes `from`: the way back from a split the analysis made, where a conditional jump inside a body it took for a function left half of it as a function of its own. Both are named by entry or any address inside them, as `ghidra_function` lists them; the answer gives the survivor's entry, name and size. Merging a function into itself, or one that is already part of the other, is refused.

from.description: The function that becomes part of it.

into.description: The function that keeps its entry and name.

module.description: The module: the SHA-256 of its bytes, as `ghidra_modules` lists it.

name: ghidra_function_merge
title: Make two functions one

description: Names, and perhaps types, a local by its `storage` and, for a register, `first_use` — as `ghidra_function` lists them — or a parameter by its `ordinal`. Never by Ghidra's own name for it (`iVar4`): those renumber. Two locals that share a storage and a first use cannot be told apart — a function holds one variable per storage — and naming either is refused; say what each is in the plate comment, and name the slot itself with `shared`: the whole storage takes one name, every use of it reads by that name, and the plate says which meaning each use carries. Use a neutral name there (`PcieSizeTooSmall`), never one of the meanings. A slot whose storage a parameter also holds is refused: name the parameter by ordinal. A slot that cannot be named whole — one use stays under another name — is refused too, and nothing is changed, rather than answered as applied. With `shared`, a `HASH:…` or `unique:…` storage is refused: it is the decompiler's own temporary, made afresh by each decompile, not a slot the module holds. Without `shared`, such a local is named and typed by its storage as any other. `type` alone types it and keeps the name. After any call, read the function again: a local's `storage` can change, and a type alone gives it a `HASH:` storage. `items` does several in one call, each in a transaction of its own: the answer lists what applied and why an entry did not. A name already held is answered with the holder — its kind, address, `storage` and `first_use` — and those rename the holder, even one the decompiler no longer shows (the answer then says `stale: true`); freeing the name is what lets the local take it. A `first_use` that is no longer the variable's is refused with what the storage holds now, since a retype can merge locals: list them again. A type the decompiler does not take is refused and nothing is changed.

first_use.description: For a register local: the address of its first use.

function.description: The function's entry address; with `items`, the function they all belong to.

items.description: Several variables of the function in one call.

first_use.description: For a register local: the address of its first use.

name.description: The new name; leave it out to type only.

ordinal.description: Or a parameter by its position, from 0.
