name.description: The new name; leave it out to type only.

ordinal.description: Or a parameter by its position, from 0.

shared.description: Name the whole storage once, for a slot the decompiler shows as several variables; with this, `storage` alone names it and `first_use` is not given.

type.description: A C type for it, e.g. "EFI_PEI_SERVICES **".

name: ghidra_rename_variable
title: Name or type a parameter or a local

description: Sets the C signature of the function at `address`, the EDK2 way if wanted; with no `storage`, a 32-bit stack keeps no hole for a UINT64, and `aligned` in the answer lists the parameters that puts elsewhere than the convention did: `convention`, where it put them, `storage`, where they are (`EFI_STATUS EFIAPI Foo (IN CONST EFI_PEI_SERVICES **PeiServices)`). Types the module lacks come from the EDK2 archive or from types a review defined. For a function no calling convention fits — a linker's clone that takes an argument in EDX, or returns through a pointer in ECX — give `storage`, one place per parameter as `ghidra_function` lists storage (`["ECX:4", "Stack[0x4]:4"]`), and `return_storage` if the result is not where the convention puts it (`EDX:4,EAX:4` for 64 bits, high part first, `void`). Then no dummy parameter is needed for a register the function does not read. A convention that does not give that storage is dropped, so the C prints none against it. A function analysis left at `unknown`, for which the decompiler writes a warning into its C, moves to `default`, which names no convention and does not say the function follows one; `convention_stays_unknown` in the answer says why not, when that would move a parameter.

module.description: The module: the SHA-256 of its bytes, as `ghidra_modules` lists it.

reason.description: Why the signature is this one. Kept as `signature_reason`, apart from the name's reason.

storage.description: Where each parameter is, in order: "EDX:4", "Stack[0x4]:4".

name: ghidra_signature
title: Set a function's signature

description: Sets the comment of `kind` at `address`, replacing the one there; empty `text` clears it. A plate comment heads a function in the C; pre and eol comments show in the C too. A comment is printed where the decompiler prints the instruction it sits on: a step folded into one expression (`&&`, a nested call) may show at the start of that block, or not at all — so a step is safest at the first instruction of its block, and the plate carries what the body cannot show. `items` writes several in one call, each in a transaction of its own.

module.description: The module: the SHA-256 of its bytes, as `ghidra_modules` lists it.

name: ghidra_comment
title: Write a comment

description: Extends the body of `function` to `end` (exclusive), for a body the analysis ended at an instruction it took for the end of the flow, such as INT1: the last instruction is set to fall through and the following instructions join the body. Refused when a function holds part of the range or the range is not whole decoded instructions.

end.description: The first address past the new body.

function.description: The function, by entry or any address inside it.

module.description: The module: the SHA-256 of its bytes, as `ghidra_modules` lists it.

name: ghidra_function_extend
title: Extend a body cut short

description: Decodes the instructions in [`start`, `end`) again from `start`, in the mode already there: the correction for a boundary the analysis got wrong, where it decoded from a byte inside an instruction. An instruction reaching into the range goes too. The answer lists the `instructions` now there and the `functions` whose bodies were fixed. A function whose entry now falls inside an instruction was cut at a false boundary: one Ghidra named is removed (`functions_removed`), one a review named stays and is reported (`entries_inside_instructions`) for `ghidra_function_delete` or `ghidra_function_merge`. Defined data in the range is refused: clear it first. For 16-bit code in a 32-bit module use `ghidra_code_mode`.

end.description: The first address past the range: [start, end).

module.description: The module: the SHA-256 of its bytes, as `ghidra_modules` lists it.

reason.description: What shows the boundary was wrong.

start.description: The address the true instruction starts at.

name: ghidra_redecode
title: Decode a range of code again

description: Reads the code in [`start`, `end`) as 16-bit or as 32-bit x86. A 32-bit module holds 16-bit code at its reset vector (real mode, before the switch to protected mode), which Ghidra decodes as 32-bit and so gets wrong: overlapping instructions, nonsense C. The instructions in the range are cleared and decoded again from `start` in the given size, without leaving the range; functions there get their bodies fixed. Addresses stay offsets: real-mode segments are not modelled, so a `cs:[F490h]` operand names F490h, not where it lands. `ghidra_disassembly` marks 16-bit instructions `bits: 16`. Defined data in the range is refused: clear it first.

end.description: The first address past it: the range is [start, end).

module.description: The module: the SHA-256 of its bytes, as `ghidra_modules` lists it.

reason.description: Why, in a few words: what shows the code is 16-bit.

start.description: The first address of the code, e.g. "0x9DFE6E0".

name: ghidra_code_mode
title: Read a range as 16-bit or 32-bit code

description: Names a constant an instruction holds — an I/O port (`PCI_CONFIG_ADDRESS` for 0xCF8), an MSR or register index, a magic value — as a Ghidra equate on that operand; the disassembly and the C show the name instead of the number, also where the number reaches an `out()` through a register. `value` picks the immediate operand that holds it, never a displacement in `[reg+1]`; `operand` picks one by index instead, and is how a displacement is named. Empty `name` removes it. One name stands for one value: a name already used for another is refused. A number the code computes (`ADD DL,4` to reach 0xCFC) is in no operand and gets a comment instead. Give every name an `enum` that groups it (`FCH_IO_PORT`, `AMD_MSR`, `LPC_DECODE_BITS`) and a `comment`: what the name stands for and where that is known from (a spec and its section, a coreboot or EDK2 header, the PPR, or `not confirmed`). The app shows the comment when the reader clicks the name, and the enum is shared with the next module reviewed, so a name given once brings its comment along: later, `name` and `enum` are enough. One value has one name in an enum. Instead of `address`, `functions` with `value` names that value wherever those functions hold it as an immediate operand; the answer lists `applied`, each address with its instruction, `skipped` operands, which keep another name they already have, and `not_immediate`, where those functions hold the value as an address, which is not named. A small value is held by unrelated instructions too: `dry_run: true` answers the same and writes nothing, so read the instructions first and name by `address` where only some are meant. `items` takes several operands in one call, each `address` with its own `operand`, `value` or `name` over the call's own, all or none; that is the way to name a displacement in many places. `in_c` says whether the function's C now prints the name, `not_in_c` lists the names of `items` it does not: an equate stands on the instruction, and the C can print something else, such as an enum member the operand's type chose.

comment.description: What the name stands for and its source; replaces the member's comment.

dry_run.description: With `functions`: answer what would be named and write nothing.

enum.description: The enum the name is a member of; made when missing.

enum_comment.description: What the enum groups, e.g. "FCH legacy I/O ports".

functions.description: Functions by entry address, instead of `address`; needs `value`.

items.description: Several operands, each {address, operand or value, and optionally name, enum, comment}.

module.description: The module: the SHA-256 of its bytes, as `ghidra_modules` lists it.

name.description: A C identifier, in the module's convention; empty removes it.

operand.description: Or the operand by its index, from 0.

value.description: The constant, e.g. "0xCF8", to pick the operand that holds it.

name: ghidra_equate
title: Name a constant in an instruction

description: Tags the function containing `address`, as the other function writes find it. A library tag marks code the module statically links in that the automatic detection did not recognise, and says whose: `library.edk2` (EDK2's MdePkg libraries — `CopyMem`, HobLib, PeiServicesLib, BaseLib's math), `library.amd` (AGESA's own libraries — LibAmd I/O, assert, IDS debug print) or `library.intel` (FSP and Reference Code libraries). Which one, and when a vendor routine is the module's own work rather than a library, is decided by the criteria in the skill's "Library functions". The exported code artifact records a function carrying the tag at the `library` review level with that kind, complete as it is. A function holds one library tag: a new one replaces it; the bare `library` is refused. An empty `tag`, or `none`, removes the library tag. The answer lists the function's tags, sorted, with `library` and `library_kind`.

address.description: The function's entry address, or any address inside it.

module.description: The module: the SHA-256 of its bytes, as `ghidra_modules` lists it.

tag.description: The tag: library.edk2, library.amd or library.intel; empty or "none" removes the library tag.

name: ghidra_function_tag
title: Tag a function

description: Names and/or types the datum at `address`, e.g. a GUID or a table. An empty `name` removes the label there, a leftover under a type that now names the place. A type laid over decoded instructions is refused, naming them, unless `clear_code: true`: they go, the function holding them gives those bytes up, and `code_cleared` says so. An address outside the image, such as an MMIO register, takes a name and `outside_memory` says so: the C prints it where the code uses that address, and `ghidra_data` and the artifact's symbols do not list it.

clear_code.description: Remove instructions the type covers and shorten the body.

module.description: The module: the SHA-256 of its bytes, as `ghidra_modules` lists it.

name.description: Its name; empty removes the label.

name: ghidra_set_data
title: Name or type a datum

description: Writes the module's description — Markdown, what the module is for, how it works and how it is built — kept in the project and published with the review as an object of its own, which the app shows beside the code. With `section`, `text` replaces the body of that `## ` section only (added at the end if missing, or beside the section `before` or `after` names; either alone moves the section); without it, `text` is the whole description. Empty `text` is refused; `delete: true`, without `text`, removes the section named, or the whole description, and the answer says which in `removed`. With `section`, `old_text` and `new_text` change one string inside that section without sending the rest; refused unless `old_text` occurs there exactly once. Up to 256 KiB. The answer names the sections and the size, not the text: `ghidra_description` reads it. It is an article for a service technician who does not program: plain prose, every abbreviation expanded in parentheses at its first mention, routines by what they do rather than by address; no function inventories, decompiler artefacts, revision history or review status — the app and the store hold those. Its sections, in this order, headed exactly so: `# <ModuleName>` and a short summary; `## What it is` (kind of file, whose, stage of start-up, the board and the module's place in the firmware — never the dump file it was read from); `## What it does`; `## Execution flow` (the main chains as short ordered walks; the events it registers for, when each fires, what it does; each chain and event links its main function or two, helpers left out); `## Interactions`; `## Inside the module`; `## Failures` (codes, messages, what the bench sees); `## Known problems` (with their practical effect); `## Terms` (only the narrow terms specific to this module that the article uses, in full: what each is, where it sits, why it matters here; common terms a technician knows, such as BIOS, USB, CMOS, UEFI, Variable, stay out). A section with nothing to say yet is left out. A link `[Name](0xADDRESS)` is optional outside `Execution flow`; a sentence must read without it. Say what is not proven. Markdown: headings, paragraphs, `-` and `1.` lists, tables, fenced code, `code`, **bold**, *italic*, links.

after.description: The section this `section` goes just after.

before.description: The section this `section` goes just before.

delete.description: Removes the section named, or the whole description. Takes no `text`.

module.description: The module: the SHA-256 of its bytes, as `ghidra_modules` lists it.

old_text.description: A string in `section` to change; it must occur there exactly once. Goes with `new_text`, takes no `text`.

section.description: The `## ` heading whose body `text` replaces, e.g. "Execution flow".

text.description: The Markdown: the whole description, or one section's body without its heading.

name: ghidra_describe
title: Write the module's description

description: Adds a structure, union, enum or typedef from C to the module, shared with modules opened after the next publish. Write the tag: `typedef struct _NAME { … } NAME;`. Without `c`, `name` picks a type the module or its archives hold. `description` says what the type is and where its layout is known from; `comments` gives fields or enum members theirs — what each holds and its source. The app shows them when the reader clicks the type or a field; an empty comment removes one. Comments are set after the C, which drops its own — a type defined again keeps its fields' comments and its description, and the answer says how many comments came back (`comments_kept`; it counts a redefinition, so it is 0 when no `c` is given), whether the C declares what the program already held (`unchanged`) and gives the type's `size`. A structure is laid out by the compiler spec unless the C says otherwise: `#pragma pack(1)` … `#pragma pack()` is how a packed record is written, and `size` beside the field offsets is how a wrong layout shows. `delete: true` with `name` removes a type the program holds — a probe or a mistake — so a publish cannot carry it; a type an archive holds is refused. With `shared: true` and a `reason` it takes a type out of the shared review archive instead: a name that turned out false. The typedef and its tag go together, and it is refused while another archive type uses them, naming those. Who and why are recorded and shown by `ghidra_type_definition` (`withdrawn`). Modules that took the type keep their copy, but no module opened after it gets it, and a publish cannot bring it back — it reads as a `type_conflicts` entry whose origin says `withdrawn`, and `take_type_conflicts` does not override that. Owners already running hold their copy of the archive until they restart. `ghidra_type_uses` lists what still names it, to walk and correct.

comments.description: A comment per field or enum member, by its name.

delete.description: Remove the type `name` from the program. No `c` with it.

description.description: What the type is, and its source.

module.description: The module: the SHA-256 of its bytes, as `ghidra_modules` lists it.

name.description: Without `c`: the type to describe, comment or delete.

reason.description: With `shared`: why the name is withdrawn. Required, and recorded.

shared.description: With `delete`: from the shared review archive, not the program.

name: ghidra_type
title: Define a type

description: The module's functions against the shared registry of reviewed library functions, matched by body (Ghidra's Function ID: the code with relocated addresses masked, and its constants). `applied`: functions carrying the current version of their entry. `to_apply`: matches that apply by themselves — `ghidra_open` applies them, and `ghidra_library_apply` without `address` does: an unnamed function takes the whole entry (`whole`); one a review named takes the entry's name, its old name kept in the reason, and only what its review left empty (`fill`); a newer version replaces one applied and not edited since; a body that differs from an entry only in the codes an assert routine is called with is a `variant` of it. `edited`: applied, then edited — the review's now. `candidates`: bodies of an entry's shape with other constants, each difference listed (`value`, `entry_value`, `assert`): other functions unless a review says why the values make no difference. `declined`: entries a review refused for the function. With `id`: one entry — its index row, its review, its history and `gaps`, what its review lacks, read from the review itself; `library_registry` reads the `function_parts` left out of the review. A match's `gaps` are the function's own missing parts as the last published analysis recorded them, and `entry_gaps` the entry's, so a decision to apply, replace or take can be made without opening either — and the two are read in the same words.

id.description: An entry's id, as `library_registry` or a match lists it: read that entry.

module.description: The module: the SHA-256 of its bytes, as `ghidra_modules` lists it.

name: ghidra_library
title: Match a module against the library registry

description: The name changes in the entry, its signatures and its stored C, not in comments or in other entries' C. A library function's name is unique in the registry, and it goes by what the functions mean, not by who published first. When a publish answers `library.name_conflicts`, read the entry that holds the name (`library_registry` with its `id`) beside the new function. If the name fits the new function, or fits neither well, give the entry the narrower name its code earns with this tool, and publish again; otherwise rename the new function. The `reason` says what the review found, and the history keeps it. Every module takes the new name at its next open. The text of the entry's recorded `function.c` keeps the old name until a new C is recorded; a reader through the registry sees the new one. `dry_run: true` answers the same and writes nothing.

dry_run.description: Answer what the rename would do and write nothing.

id.description: The entry to rename, as a name conflict's `held_by` gives it.

module.description: The module: the SHA-256 of its bytes, as `ghidra_modules` lists it.

name.description: The narrower name, free in the registry.

reason.description: What the review of both functions found.

name: ghidra_library_rename
title: Give a library registry entry a narrower name

description: A library function depends on no module: it refers to no data but a constant of its own library's source, and calls only library functions. A body that does not qualify leaves the registry with this tool: with `body`, that body alone; without, the whole entry, and its name is free. A publish does not offer it again. A module whose function took it or was tagged with it keeps the text at its next open, and the function stops being library. The history stays. `ghidra_library_restore` takes a wrong decision back. `dry_run: true` answers the same and writes nothing.

body.description: One of its bodies; omit for the whole entry.

dry_run.description: Answer what would be done and write nothing.

module.description: The module: the SHA-256 of its bytes, as `ghidra_modules` lists it.

reason.description: What in the code ties it to a module.

name: ghidra_library_take_out
title: Give a body back to its modules

description: Takes back a `ghidra_library_take_out`: the body returns to its entry, or the entry returns with it. The name must still be free. `dry_run: true` answers the same and writes nothing.

body.description: The body key, as the index's `taken_out` lists it.

dry_run.description: Answer what would be done and write nothing.

module.description: The module: the SHA-256 of its bytes, as `ghidra_modules` lists it.

name: ghidra_library_restore
title: Take a body back into the registry

description: Different bodies are different functions. One body of an entry becomes an entry of its own, under the name its code earns, starting from the review they shared; correct its text from a module that holds it. The body the entry is keyed by stays: give it its name with `ghidra_library_rename`, and split the others off. `dry_run: true` answers the same and writes nothing.

dry_run.description: Answer what would be done and write nothing.

module.description: The module: the SHA-256 of its bytes, as `ghidra_modules` lists it.

name.description: Its name, free in the registry.

name: ghidra_library_split
title: Make one body of an entry its own entry

description: A body that refers to data enters the registry only if the data is a constant defined in its own library's source. Cite the file and line after comparing the bytes with that source; the registry cannot check it and keeps who said so. Give `id` for an entry's bodies, or `body` for one, also before its first publish: a publish's `library.not_library` names the key. A GUID never qualifies. A body with two constants has two citations: another file or line adds one, the same file and line replaces it, `remove: true` takes it away. `citations` says which, with what was replaced; the registry keeps that. `dry_run: true` answers the same and writes nothing.

dry_run.description: Answer what would be done and write nothing.

file.description: The source file, by its path in its tree.

id.description: The entry; omit when naming a `body`.

line.description: The line that defines the constant.

module.description: The module: the SHA-256 of its bytes, as `ghidra_modules` lists it.

remove.description: Take this file and line away.

name: ghidra_library_cite
title: Cite the source of a body's constant

description: Applies the registry's entries to the module, each in a transaction of its own, and answers each in `results`: `renamed` (from, to), `filled`, `differences` the function's review keeps, `unplaced` (a variable or comment the function has no place for), `leftovers` — the gaps the function still keeps after the apply, so a local it left unnamed says so at once — and `marked` when the function is now the entry's. Without `address`: every match `ghidra_library` lists in `to_apply`. With `address`: that function — a candidate only with `reason` (why its other constants make no difference: it becomes a variant of the entry at the next publish); `replace: true` puts the entry's review in place of a review that differs or was edited since; `leftovers` accompany an apply that names `address`, and a bulk apply leaves them out (the reading decompiles each function it answers); `fields` takes only the parts named — signature (return type, convention, parameter types), names (the function's and its parameters'), locals, plate, comments — and keeps the rest of the function's. `dry_run: true` answers the same and writes nothing: each entry is applied in its transaction and rolled back, so a `replace` can be read before it is made. `decline: true` refuses the entry for the function (`id`, or the one matched), and it is not offered again. A difference a review keeps is settled by keeping it, or by publishing it as the entry's next version (`ghidra_publish` with `take_library_conflicts` and a reason). A match's `gaps` are the function's own missing parts and `entry_gaps` the entry's, so the two reviews can be compared before either is changed.

address.description: The function's entry. Leave out to apply every match that applies by itself.

decline.description: Refuse the entry for the function at `address`.

dry_run.description: Answer what the apply would do — filled, differences, unplaced, leftovers — and write nothing.

fields.description: Take parts of the entry's review and keep the rest of the function's: signature, names, locals, plate, comments.

full.description: Answer with the functions already carrying their entry; by default only a count.

id.description: The entry, where several match the function.

module.description: The module: the SHA-256 of its bytes, as `ghidra_modules` lists it.

reason.description: Why a candidate's other constants make no difference, or why an entry is declined.

replace.description: Put the entry's review in place of the function's.

name: ghidra_library_apply
title: Apply or decline a library registry entry

description: Saves the module's program and stores its artifact and review document as the next revision: every ByteRipper reading this store shows the new names. Publishing an unchanged program is the same revision. `stale_links` lists links in comments and the description whose text is a default name (`FUN_…`) while the target now has a real one: `at` and `kind` say where, `name` is what the text should read; they are reported, not rewritten. `type_conflicts` names types another review defines differently, which stay in this module only: `ghidra_type_definition` shows both, and `type_conflict_origins` names the module that wrote the shared copy. `take_type_conflicts: true` replaces the shared copy of each conflicting type with this module's — the answer to a layout that was published wrong, and never an enum, whose clashing member means one of the two reviews is wrong. The types replaced come back as `type_conflicts_taken`, a typedef and the structure it names each named, since the archive holds them separately. A type made of a replaced one follows it and is not named, so a take can name fewer types than `type_conflicts` listed; a dry run with both flags merges into a copy of the archive and answers what the publish would. The library registry is offered every function tagged `library.<kind>` whose review meets the bar of a finished function: `library` says which bodies became entries (`added`), new versions (`updated` — a change to a function that was the entry's current version, from any module: no module holds an entry), were the same (`unchanged`), or hold another review not made on the current version (`conflicts`: the entry's name and version, the version this review was made on as `base`, who published the current one, and the name this module proposes); `library_below_bar` lists the tagged functions short of the bar with their gaps. `take_library_conflicts: true` with `library_reason` makes this module's review of every conflicting body the entry's next version; a list of entry ids takes those alone, each with its own reason in `library_reason` given as an object — a reason is required for each and kept in the entry's history. The conflicts not taken come back in `conflicts`, with the version this review was based on as `base`. A change names its `module` and `reason` on its row and in the entry's history, so a publish that would move an entry with no reason is refused and stores nothing, naming the entries in the refusal. Give each one in `entry_reasons`, an object of entry id to why this module changes it. A first version, an unchanged entry and a taken conflict with its reason need none; a take that names the entry also speaks for a change on its current version, and a function's own reason does only when its name or signature is all that moved. A store that predates this rule is refused, since it would take the change with no reason. By default the answer carries only what the publish changed; `full: true` adds the list of entries it left as they were. `dry_run: true` answers the same without storing (its artifact hash is taken before the registry's states and marks, so a publish that touches the registry stores another): the artifact's counts, the revision it would become, the description's size, the type conflicts, and — with the library decision given as it would be to the publish — `library`, what the registry offer would do: the entries it would add or move to their next version, the conflicts it would leave, the entries that need a reason in `library.needs_reason` with the refusal in `library_refused`, and the same refusal a take of an entry that is not in conflict gets, in `library_error`. The export is done, so it costs what a publish costs. Publishing is the point another host sees the work; the owner also writes the program out when it idles out, is stopped or gets a signal — not after every change — so only an owner killed outright or crashed loses what came after the last publish.

dry_run.description: Answer what a publish would store — counts, the revision, the conflicts — and store nothing.

entry_reasons.description: Why this module changes each entry this publish moves: an object of entry id to reason, kept in the entry's history.

full.description: Answer with every entry the publish left as it was; by default only what changed.

library_reason.description: Why this module's review is the better one: one text for take_library_conflicts: true, or an object of entry id to reason for a list.

module.description: The module: the SHA-256 of its bytes, as `ghidra_modules` lists it.

take_library_conflicts.description: Take the conflicts this module's review wins: true for every one, or a list of entry ids for those alone.

take_type_conflicts.description: Replace the shared copy of each conflicting type with this module's. An enum is never taken.

name: ghidra_publish
title: Publish the review

description: Publishes what the project holds and the store has not got, this session's changes or an earlier session's, and gives the module's write lease back, so another session or a person can write. With nothing changed it publishes nothing. The module's owner stays up until it has been idle for a while, so a read or the next open costs no start; a later write takes a new lease. A publish that would move a library entry with no reason is refused and the lease stays: give `entry_reasons` to `ghidra_publish` first.

module.description: The module: the SHA-256 of its bytes, as `ghidra_modules` lists it.

name: ghidra_done
title: End the review session

description: Stops the module's owner and moves its kept Ghidra project to the Trash, and answers where it went. Nothing of the analysis store is touched: the module's revisions, their artifacts and the shared review types stay, and the module opens again from its bytes and is analysed afresh. This is for a project whose program cannot be put right — an analysis gone wrong that a re-run should replace. Publish what is worth keeping first: the store is the only part that survives.

module.description: The module: the SHA-256 of its bytes, as `ghidra_modules` lists it.

name: ghidra_forget
title: Let a module's kept project go

description: Overwrites bytes in a document open in a tab, as one step of its undo named by `label` — write the label in the person's language, it is what their Edit menu offers to undo. The bytes replace as many as they are, never inserting or deleting: a write past the end of the file is refused. The written bytes show red until the person saves, and the dump scrolls to them. `expect` makes the write conditional: the bytes there now must be these, or nothing is written and the answer says what is there. Needs the person's permission — Settings ▸ Agent, "Let agents edit open files"; without it the write is refused. Never saves; checksums are not updated — use a module's fix, such as `uefi_fix_checksum`.

bytes.description: The bytes as hex, e.g. "DE AD BE EF" or "deadbeef"; at most 64 KiB.

document.description: The document's id from `documents`. Default: the focused one.

expect.description: The bytes that must be at `offset` now, as hex. Optional.

label.description: What the change is, for the undo step: "Enable the debug option".

name: write
title: Write bytes

description: Copies a range of one of a tab's two files over the same addresses in the other — what Edit ▸ Copy to Other Pane (⌥⌘C) does with the selection. The bytes go from file to file inside ByteRipper and never through you, so there is no size limit: a whole region or volume is one call. Overwrites only: a range past the end of the other file is refused, never grown. One undo step in the receiving file, named by `label`; the copied bytes show red until the person saves, and its pane scrolls to them. The answer says how many bytes actually changed and where in the firmware the range lies. Needs the person's permission — Settings ▸ Agent, "Let agents edit open files". Never saves; checksums are not updated.

document.description: The file to copy from: one of a tab's two files, by its id from `documents`. Default: the focused one.

label.description: What the copy is, for the undo step, in the person's language. Default: Copy to Other Pane.

name: copy_to_other_pane
title: Copy bytes to the other pane

description: Puts a part's bytes back into the document it was opened from — File ▸ Update in Parent. The part's codec says how: a copy goes back as it is, a decompressed body is compressed again and the image laid out around it, a decoded block is encoded again with its checksum. One undo step in the parent; the parent's bytes show red until the person saves, and the parent is shown where they landed. A part with nothing new answers `updated: false`. Refused, with nothing written: when the parent is closed or read-only; when the codec cannot put the bytes back (a part whose length changed, a body that no longer fits once compressed — the answer gives the codec's reason); when the parent changed while the update was worked out (call again); and when the bytes the part came from have changed in the parent since it was opened — then ask the person, and call again with `overwrite_changed_source: true` only if they agree. A refusal that is a caution rather than an impossibility — a part of the BIOS image an AMD PSP decompresses itself, which the PSP may not accept once compressed again — says so: then explain the risk to the person, and call again with `update_anyway: true` only if they agree. Needs the person's permission — Settings ▸ Agent, "Let agents edit open files". Never saves.

document.description: The part's id from `documents`. Default: the focused one.

overwrite_changed_source.description: Overwrite the parent's bytes even though they changed since the part was opened. Only after the person said so. Default false.

update_anyway.description: Go on past the codec's caution, as the dialog's Update Anyway does — the PSP's BIOS image compressed again although it is not known whether the PSP accepts it. Only after the person said so. Default false.

name: update_in_parent
title: Update in Parent

description: The Intel ME / CSME / TXE / SPS firmware in the image, as the ME Analyzer panel's Summary tab gives it: family, version, release, type, SKU, the platform, the security version (SVN), whether the firmware database knows this build, and the analysis's messages (a corrupted partition, a module whose hash fails, an update that will not apply). `tone` marks a verdict: good, caution or bad. A value of "Coming soon" is a row this engine does not answer yet. The File System State row carries `basis`: what each of the three steps that decide it found (the reserved MFS files, whether the EFS volume holds files, the configuration partitions), which step decided it, `complete: false` when a step that could have raised the state could not be taken — an EFS partition that could not be read — and an `explanation`. Say the basis when you report the state: Configured with an unreadable EFS is not the same fact as Configured with an empty one. The first call on a dump analyses its ME region, which takes a second or two.

document.description: The document's id from `documents`. Default: the focused one.

name: me_summary
title: ME summary

description: The structure the ME engine decoded, as the ME Analyzer panel's Full Info tab shows it: the partition table, partitions, code partition manifests and modules, the MFS or EFS file system and its files, the configuration records, the checksums. Without `node`, the top groups; with it, that node's fields and its children. Each node: `id` (pass it back as `node`; ids are positions, so they hold for this dump only), `title`, `subtitle`, its bytes (`start`, `end`) when it stands for some, `children` as a count, and `problem` with its lines when the panel marks one. An MFS or EFS file has no one range: its bytes are scattered over the volume's pages, so it says `stretches`, how many, and asked for as `node` lists them as `extents`, in the file's own order. Pages: `limit` is the most children on one page, a ceiling — a page also stops before the answer passes the size bound and then says `truncated: "size"`; pass `next` back as `after` until it is null. `total` counts the children.

after.description: The `next` of the page before, to go on from where it stopped.

document.description: The document's id from `documents`. Default: the focused one.

limit.description: The most items one page holds — a ceiling: a page stops sooner when the answer would pass the size bound, and says so with `truncated: "size"`. Default 100, at most 400.

node.description: A node id such as "2.0.3" from an earlier answer. Default: the top.

name: me_tree
title: ME structure

description: The Firmware Interface Table as the FIT panel reads it: where the pointer at the top of the image leads, the table's place and checksum, and its rows — type, address, size, version and what the row points at (a microcode with its CPUID, revision and date; a region the tree names). `problems` are the specification's rules the table breaks, each with its row and address. The Top Swap backup's copy of the table follows under `backup` when the image keeps one. With `entry` (the row's place, 0 is the header) that row's every field as well. Whether a newer microcode exists is the panel's to say, not this answer's.

document.description: The document's id from `documents`. Default: the focused one.

entry.description: A row's place in the table, 0 for the header: its fields in full.

name: fit_table
title: FIT table

description: The Intel microcode the online collection at github.com/platomav/CPUMicrocodes holds — the catalogue the FIT panel's Add Microcode lists — read from the file names, so nothing is downloaded. Each file: `path` (pass it to `fit_add_microcode` or `fit_replace_microcode`), CPUID, platform mask, revision, date, `production` (false for a pre-release), size. One update with an extended signature table is filed once under each processor it serves. With `in_image`, only files for processors the image's FIT microcodes serve — their extended tables' included — and `installed` says each microcode row's processors and platforms, its revision and how it stands against the catalogue (`latest`, `outdated` with the newest revision, `undecided` where a newer file's platform mask only partly meets the installed one's, so the board's own platform decides, `not_rated`); a file then says which rows it `serves_rows` and whether it is `newer_than_installed`. `cpuid` narrows by the CPUID's first digits. Pages: `limit` is a ceiling — a page also stops before the answer passes the size bound and says `truncated: "size"`; pass `next` back as `after` until it is null.

after.description: The `next` of the page before, to go on from where it stopped.

cpuid.description: Only files whose CPUID starts with this, e.g. "906E".

document.description: The document's id from `documents`. Default: the focused one.

in_image.description: Only files for processors the image's microcodes serve, and how each row stands. Default false.

latest_only.description: Only the newest revision for each CPUID and platform mask. Default false.

limit.description: The most items one page holds — a ceiling: a page stops sooner when the answer would pass the size bound, and says so with `truncated: "size"`. Default 50, at most 300.

production_only.description: Leave out pre-release files. Default false.

name: microcode_catalogue
title: Microcode catalogue

description: The structure of a firmware image as the UEFI Structure panel shows it: regions, volumes, files, sections, NVRAM stores and the rest. Without `node`, the top of the tree and a one-line summary of the image; with it, that node and its children. `depth` (1–3) goes further down. Each node: `id` (pass it back as `node` — never show it to the person), `label` (what to call it to the person: its name, with its addresses where the name is only a kind such as Unused), on a file on disk `link` (the label as a Markdown link that opens the node in ByteRipper — write it where you name the node), type, subtype, name, GUID, its bytes (`start`, `end`, or `in_compressed: true` when it lives inside a decompressed section and has no file address), `compressed` — a compressed section's own algorithm, or for a node it decompresses to the algorithm it came out of — and `compressed_in`, the innermost section it was decompressed out of, on every node with `in_compressed`; `encoded` ("XOR 77") for a LENV block or entry stored encoded in the file; `counterpart` and `decoded_in` for a node also open in a part (see `uefi_at`: {document, node, as}), and `children` — a count, or "unread" for a container not opened yet (asking for it opens it). With `depth` above 1 a child carries the levels under it as `below`. Pages: `limit` is the most children of `node` on one page, a ceiling — a page also stops before the answer passes the size bound and then says `truncated: "size"`; pass `next` back as `after` until it is null. A child whose levels below are too large alone comes without them, marked `truncated: "item"`; ask for it as `node`. Ids belong to the document they were listed on: a part opened with `open_part` has a tree of its own, with ids that start over (the parent's 0.3.4.1.2.5 is 0.0.5 in the decoded block), so give the `document` the id came from. Asked of the parent while the focus is on its part, or the other way round, the answer carries a `focus_note`; a refusal over an id of the other one names the document that has it.

after.description: The `next` of the page before, to go on from where it stopped.

depth.description: How many levels below the node. Default 1, at most 3.

document.description: The document's id from `documents`. Default: the focused one.

limit.description: The most items one page holds — a ceiling: a page stops sooner when the answer would pass the size bound, and says so with `truncated: "size"`. Default 100, at most 400.

node.description: A node id such as "0.2.5" from an earlier answer. Default: the top.

name: uefi_tree
title: UEFI tree

description: Everything the UEFI Structure panel's detail says about one node: its fields (header values, sizes, attributes, checksums — a wrong checksum is marked `problem`), its tables, the path of names down to it, and the parser's diagnostics inside its bytes. NVRAM variables come with their value decoded. A module with a dependency expression adds `dependencies`: the expression in words, the GUIDs it pushes, every opcode with its offset, and what does not parse.

document.description: The document's id from `documents`. Default: the focused one.

name: uefi_node
title: UEFI node

description: Finds nodes anywhere in the image — opening every volume and decompressing every section it can, which takes a few seconds on a large image the first time. Give any of: `name` (part of the name, any case; the whole name with `exact`), `guid` (exact), `type` (the Type column, e.g. "File", "Section", "Volume", "VSS entry", "NVAR entry"), `depends_on` (a PPI or protocol GUID — the files whose dependency expression pushes it, and only files). All given must match. Each match has its id and the path of names to it; `total` counts them all. Pages: `limit` is a ceiling — a page also stops before the answer passes the size bound and then says `truncated: "size"`; pass `next` back as `after` until it is null.

after.description: The `next` of the page before, to go on from where it stopped.

depends_on.description: A PPI or protocol GUID a module's dependency expression pushes.

document.description: The document's id from `documents`. Default: the focused one.

exact.description: Match the whole name rather than a part of it. Default false.

limit.description: The most items one page holds — a ceiling: a page stops sooner when the answer would pass the size bound, and says so with `truncated: "size"`. Default 50, at most 200.

name.description: Part of the node's name, any case.

type.description: The node type as the Type column shows it.

name: uefi_find
title: Find UEFI nodes

description: The chain of nodes that hold a byte of the file, outermost first — region, volume, file, section — opening the containers on the way. The last one is the innermost. Each node as `uefi_tree` gives it, with `encoded` ("XOR 77") for a LENV block or entry stored encoded and `compressed` / `compressed_in` for one inside a compressed section. A node whose bytes are also those of an open part, or of the parent of the part asked about, names its node there as `counterpart` ({document, node, as: "decoded" | "encoded" | "same"}), and `decoded_in` when that part is its LENV block opened decoded — read and show it there. Asked of the parent while the focus is on its part, or the other way round, the answer carries a `focus_note`.

document.description: The document's id from `documents`. Default: the focused one.

name: uefi_at
title: UEFI nodes at an address

description: Checks every checksum the UEFI Structure panel checks — a volume's header checksum, a file's header and data checksums, a microcode's, an AMD PSP or BIOS directory's — in the whole image or under `node`, opening every volume and decompressing every section it can, and lists the nodes whose checksums are wrong: which field, what is stored and what it should be. A node inside a compressed section is checked against what the section decompresses to; it is marked `in_compressed` and cannot be fixed in place. `checked` counts the nodes that carry a checksum, `wrong` those listed. `uefi_fix_checksum` puts them right, one node or all at once. Pages: `limit` is a ceiling — a page also stops before the answer passes the size bound and then says `truncated: "size"`; pass `next` back as `after` until it is null.

after.description: The `next` of the page before, to go on from where it stopped.

document.description: The document's id from `documents`. Default: the focused one.

limit.description: The most items one page holds — a ceiling: a page stops sooner when the answer would pass the size bound, and says so with `truncated: "size"`. Default 50, at most 200.

node.description: Check only under this node, e.g. "0.2". Default: the whole image.

name: uefi_checksums
title: Check the UEFI checksums

description: Judges by their bytes the nodes the parser cannot name — Padding (the flash map's Unused, Unknown and named areas among them) and Raw files and sections — under `node` (default: the BIOS region), in address order. A node its children divide is replaced by them; one whose only child covers it whole stays, naming the child as `inner`. Each: `node`, `name`, `type`, `subtype`, `guid`, `start`, `end`, `size`; `fill` (the share of 0xFF and 0x00 bytes), `first_nonfill` and `last_nonfill` (the first and the last other byte); `class` — `empty` (at least 99% fill), `text` (most of the other bytes are ASCII or UTF-16LE strings of 4 characters or more), `code` (x86-64 instructions, by a heuristic: frequent REX.W moves, calls and returns, or a PE image), else `data`; and up to five `strings` with their addresses. The bytes themselves are never answered: `read` or `uefi_node_data` read them. An area whose name in the flash map says MSDM, Password or Key gives its class and sizes, no strings, and `redacted: true`. `kinds` picks the node types (the Type or Subtype column), default Padding and Raw; `min_size` leaves out smaller nodes. Pages: `limit`, `after` as in `uefi_find`. With `survey`, the same area across a folder of dumps.

after.description: The `next` of the page before, to go on from where it stopped.

document.description: The document's id from `documents`. Default: the focused one.

kinds.description: Node types to take, as the Type or Subtype column shows them. Default ["Padding", "Raw"].

limit.description: The most items one page holds — a ceiling: a page stops sooner when the answer would pass the size bound, and says so with `truncated: "size"`. Default 50, at most 200.

min_size.description: Leave out nodes smaller than this. Default 0x100.

node.description: Scan under this node, e.g. "0.2". Default: the BIOS region, or the whole image.

name: region_scan
title: Scan the nameless areas

description: The image's DMI areas — where the firmware keeps the board's identity: serial numbers, UUID, model — as the UEFI Structure panel's DMI button finds them. It opens every container in the file, but no compressed section. Each area: `layout` ("Lenovo DMI store", "GPNV store", "Acer DMI", "Panasonic DMI" — the Type column calls these Padding — or "HP DMI", a VSS entry that may be one the store marks deleted, as most HP boards keep it, or "Apple DMI", a SysF store), its node as `uefi_tree` gives it (`id`, `label`, `link`, `start`, `end`, `encoded` for an XORed LENV block), `size`, `path`, and the panel's `fields` and `tables` for it; `uefi_node` on its children reads further, `uefi_node_data` reads the bytes. The parser finds a DMI area only by its algorithms for the dump layouts it knows: Lenovo's DMI store (an LDBG change log and two LENV blocks), AMI's GPNV store as ASUS writes it, Acer's 8 KiB DMI area, Panasonic's DMI area (a MEI_ header, a directory and records), and HP's HP_MUD variable in the main VSS2 store, with BuildId, FactoryConfig (the feature byte) and HP_TAGS (the asset tracking number) beside it — what HP's BCU reports, and Apple's SysF store of the Mac's serial number (ssn), configuration code (hwc) and sales order number (son), with the board's serial read from the names of its calibration variables. An area that is not found is not therefore absent from the dump: it may be in a layout the parser does not know, or a known one that is damaged, wiped or moved so its checks fail. So an empty `areas` means only that the parser recognised none — say so to the person, never that the dump has no DMI; `region_scan` judges the nameless areas by their bytes, which is where to look next. With `survey`, group a folder of dumps by "total" or "areas.0.layout" — the whole answer holds each board's own serials, so no two dumps would share a group.

document.description: The document's id from `documents`. Default: the focused one.

name: uefi_dmi
title: DMI area

description: The NVRAM variables the image keeps, from every VSS, VSS2, NVAR, Dell DVAR and GPNV store — those inside compressed sections too, so the first call on a large image takes a few seconds. `stores` lists the stores the rows are in, with how many variables each holds (`variables`) and, apart from them, how many it no longer holds (`deleted`). One row per variable: the copy that stands for it now. `copies` above 1 says the store still keeps earlier values (`uefi_node` on the entry lists them); `deleted: true` is a variable the store no longer holds, listed only with `deleted`. Each row: name, GUID, the store's and the entry's node ids, the value's bytes (`start`, `end`, `size`), and `value` — the value read as its type (a number, text, a boot option, a device path, a signature list) or as hex when it is short. Other stores (EVSA, Apple SysF, flash maps) are in `uefi_tree`. Pages: `limit` is a ceiling — a page also stops before the answer passes the size bound and then says `truncated: "size"`; pass `next` back as `after` until it is null. `total` counts every row. A row too large alone comes without its `value`, marked `truncated: "item"`; `read` its bytes.

after.description: The `next` of the page before, to go on from where it stopped.

deleted.description: Also list variables the store no longer holds. Default false.

document.description: The document's id from `documents`. Default: the focused one.

limit.description: The most items one page holds — a ceiling: a page stops sooner when the answer would pass the size bound, and says so with `truncated: "size"`. Default 80, at most 300.

name.description: Part of the variable's name, any case.

store.description: Only this store's variables: its node id from an earlier answer.

name: variables
title: NVRAM variables

description: Reads a node's bytes as `read` reads a document's — rows of 16 with their address, text, or integers — at addresses inside the node's `part` (`body` by default, `header`, or `all`), from 0. Works for a node inside a compressed section too, which has no file address and which `read` cannot reach: its bytes are what the tree decompressed it to, and `source` says which compressed section in the file they came out of. For a compressed section itself, part `decompressed` is what it decompresses to — the buffer its children are in. `size` is the whole part's, to read on by `offset`; at most 4096 bytes at a time. `ranges` reads several places of the part in one call, each as its own row of the answer's `ranges`, 4096 bytes in all. A node of the file gives `file_start` as well: its bytes are the document's at that address, unsaved edits included, and `read`, `reveal` and `write` work there. `find_bytes` with `node` searches the node and everything decompressed or decoded under it.

document.description: The document's id from `documents`. Default: the focused one.

endian.description: For u16, u32 and u64. Default "little".

length.description: How many bytes. Default 256, at most 4096.

offset.description: Where to start inside the part. Default 0x0.

part.description: Which bytes of the node. Default "body". `offset` counts from this part's start: a `find_bytes` match's `body_offset` goes with "body", its `node_offset` with "all".

ranges.description: Instead of `offset` and `length`: several places, each "offset+length", such as "0x100+0x20"; at most 64.

name: uefi_node_data
title: UEFI node bytes

description: Sets the files of the ME file systems of two documents side by side — `document` and `against` — by what each volume calls them (an MFS file's index, an EFS file's file ID) and by what they hold, not by address. An MFS volume moves its pages to spread the wear, so one machine's two dumps keep the same file in different places, and `diff` over the MFS partition mostly finds pages moved; this says which files changed. Content is compared without the Integrity table a protected file ends with; that table changes whenever the engine writes the file again, so it is reported apart (`integrity_differs`). Answers `counts` (same — and of those, `moved` and `rewritten` — different, only in one, incomplete), the files that differ with both sizes and how many content bytes differ, and the files only in one dump. `name` is the file table's path or name where it gives one. A volume that could not be read on either side is under `not_compared` with the reason, and its files are not listed as missing. `incomplete` is a file whose chain of chunks broke off, so what it holds is not known whole. With `extents`, each listed file says where it is stored in each dump: the stretches in the file's own order, which `read` reads back. Pages: the lists are one sequence — `different`, `only_in_document`, `only_in_against`, `incomplete` — and `limit` is the most items of it on one page, a ceiling: a page also stops before the answer passes the size bound and then says `truncated: "size"`. Pass `next` back as `after` until it is null; `counts` are of the whole comparison. A file whose extents are too many for one answer lists the first of them, marked `truncated: "item"`; `me_tree` on the file lists them. `encrypted` is the file table's flag: an encrypted file the engine wrote again with a new nonce differs in nearly every byte, so for it `different` says it was written, not that what it holds changed.

after.description: The `next` of the page before, to go on from where it stopped.

against.description: The id of the document to set beside it, from `documents` or `open_dump`.

document.description: The first document's id from `documents`. Default: the focused one.

extents.description: Say where each listed file is stored in each dump. Default false.

limit.description: The most items one page holds — a ceiling: a page stops sooner when the answer would pass the size bound, and says so with `truncated: "size"`. Default 40, at most 200.

name.description: Only files whose name contains this, any case.

volume.description: Only this volume: "mfs" or "efs". Default: both.

name: me_files_compare
title: Compare ME files

description: Sets the NVRAM variables of two documents side by side — `document` and `against` — by name and GUID, not by address, so two dumps of different boards or BIOS versions compare as well as two of one board. A name and GUID kept twice in an image (live and default stores) is paired by which time it is met. Answers the variables only in one of them, those whose values differ — with both sizes, the bytes that differ as offsets into the value, and both values read as their type — and how many are the same. Variables a store no longer holds are left out. `survey` with this tool and a fixed `against` compares a folder of dumps with one. Pages: the three lists are one sequence — `changed`, then `only_in_document`, then `only_in_against` — and `limit` is the most items of it on one page, a ceiling: a page also stops before the answer passes the size bound and then says `truncated: "size"`. Pass `next` back as `after` until it is null; `counts` and `same` are of the whole comparison. A changed variable too large alone comes without its values, marked `truncated: "item"`.

after.description: The `next` of the page before, to go on from where it stopped.

against.description: The id of the document to set beside it, from `documents` or `open_dump`.

document.description: The first document's id from `documents`. Default: the focused one.

limit.description: The most items one page holds — a ceiling: a page stops sooner when the answer would pass the size bound, and says so with `truncated: "size"`. Default 40, at most 200.

name.description: Only variables whose name contains this, any case.

name: variables_compare
title: Compare NVRAM variables

description: Writes the checksum the FIT table should have into its header row — and into the Top Swap backup's copy when that copy is the same table — as the FIT panel's Fix Checksum does, as one undo step. Refused when there is no table, when its checksum is not checked or already correct, and without the person's permission to edit.

document.description: The document's id from `documents`. Default: the focused one.

name: fit_fix_checksum
title: Fix the FIT checksum

description: Downloads a catalogue file (`path` from `microcode_catalogue`) and adds it to the FIT, as the panel's Add Microcode does, as one undo step: where a row's update already serves the same processor — its extended signature table counted — the new one takes that row's place (`change`: "replaced", with what it `replaced`), otherwise it gets a row of its own ("added"). Refused, with the reason, when the very same update is already in the table under another of its CPUIDs, when the file is not a microcode or its checksum is wrong, when the table or the run cannot grow, inside a Boot Guard IBB, when a Top Swap backup differs, and without the person's permission to edit. Says where the component went, how many microcodes behind it `moved`, the `top_swap_backup` it was made in too, and what it means for the `protected_ranges`.

document.description: The document's id from `documents`. Default: the focused one.

name: fit_add_microcode
title: Add a microcode

description: Downloads a catalogue file (`path` from `microcode_catalogue`) and puts it in the place of row `entry`'s microcode, as the panel's Replace Microcode does, as one undo step — whatever the new update's CPUID. Refused when the same update is already in the table, and when the new one serves a processor, on a shared platform, that another row's update already serves — extended signature tables counted — since the table would then hold two microcodes for one processor: that row is the one to replace. Refused too for the reasons `fit_add_microcode` gives. Says as it does what changed.

document.description: The document's id from `documents`. Default: the focused one.

entry.description: The microcode row's place in the table, from `fit_table`.

name: fit_replace_microcode
title: Replace a microcode

description: Takes row `entry` and its microcode out of the FIT, as the panel's Remove Microcode does, as one undo step: the components behind it move up into the space and the rows follow them, and the bytes freed at the end of the run are erased. Refused for the table's last microcode, inside a Boot Guard IBB, when a Top Swap backup differs, and without the person's permission to edit. Says how many `moved` and what was `erased`.

document.description: The document's id from `documents`. Default: the focused one.

entry.description: The microcode row's place in the table, from `fit_table`.

name: fit_remove_microcode
title: Remove a microcode

description: Puts checksums right — a volume's header checksum, a file's header and data checksums, a microcode's, an AMD PSP or BIOS directory's — computed by the code the UEFI Structure panel's Fix Checksum runs, and writes them as one undo step. Give `node` for one node, or `all: true` for every wrong checksum in the image (or under `node`) that can be written in place: a file that holds a volume is put right after the files inside it, over their fixed bytes. `uefi_checksums` lists the wrong ones, `uefi_node` marks one with `problem`. A node inside a compressed section is never written (the file holds those bytes compressed): refused by itself, left out of `all` and counted in `skipped_compressed`. Refused when nothing is wrong, and without the person's permission to edit.

all.description: Every wrong checksum in the image, or under `node`. Default false.

document.description: The document's id from `documents`. Default: the focused one.

node.description: The node's id, e.g. "0.2.5". With `all`, only under it.

name: uefi_fix_checksum
title: Fix UEFI checksums

The id is the one listed on the document the call goes to: a part has its own ids, not its parent's.
